recipe.history:
The prune — a dried plum — occupies an unusual position in culinary history: it is one of the world's most ancient preserved foods, deeply respected in the kitchens of multiple cultures, and yet in modern American consciousness it is haunted by unfortunate associations with institutional food and digestive medicine. This is an unearned reputation. The prune d'Agen, the French dried plum from the town of Agen in the Lot-et-Garonne department of Gascony, is one of the great luxury preserved fruits of Europe, protected by a geographical indication and prized for its complex flavor — deep and dark, with notes of caramel, dried fruit, plum wine, and a richness that resembles chocolate in its concentration. The Agen plum was introduced to France from Damascus by the Crusaders in the 12th century (hence its botanical name Prunus domestica), and the tradition of drying these plums in the stone ovens of the Gascon farmhouses after the bread baking was done dates to at least the 13th century. Gascon cooking — the cuisine of southwest France, the land of duck confit, foie gras, and Armagnac — uses prunes with extraordinary creativity, particularly in combination with pork, game, and wine-based sauces where the fruit's sweetness and acid balance the richness of the meat.

The prune's rehabilitation in serious cooking began with the broader French influence on American cuisine in the second half of the 20th century, and Julia Child's enthusiasm for the classic Gascon combination of prunes and port wine in preparations like rabbit à la périgourdine helped establish the fruit as a legitimate ingredient in the American fine dining kitchen. Prune mostarda — the Italian preparation of fruit preserved in a mustard-spiked syrup, originating in Cremona and Mantua in Lombardy — brought a further dimension: the mustard oil gives the candied fruit a sharp, almost electric bite that cuts through the sweetness and makes it a natural companion to rich meats. The prune-port wine compote and the mostarda together on a burger create a condiment combination of unusual depth: sweet, tannic, acidic, slightly sharp, with the dark, plummy undertone that elevates the beef rather than overshadowing it.

I came to prunes through Armagnac, which came to me through a bottle someone brought back from a road trip through Gascony and left at my apartment without explanation. I opened it one evening with a plate of prunes d'Agen — the combination is classic and I had read about it — and sat with both for an hour while the rain came down outside. The flavor of the Armagnac-soaked prune is one of those things that makes you feel you understand why human beings have spent thousands of years refining their food culture: the sweetness, the tannin, the caramel, the fruit, the spirit — all of it compressed into something the size of a walnut. When I eventually put a version of that flavor on a beef patty, using port wine instead of Armagnac for the compote and a jar of Italian mostarda I had been hoarding, it worked in a way that felt inevitable.

Bold, dark, complex flavors demand a bold, correctly cooked patty, and the prune-port compote and mostarda on this burger require the full depth that only medium rare beef can provide. The tannins in port wine mirror the tannins in a well-developed beef crust; the sweetness of the compote needs the savory fat of a properly cooked patty to anchor it; the sharp mustard bite of the mostarda requires the yielding, pink, juicy interior of a medium rare patty to provide contrast. At 130–135°F, the beef contributes its iron richness, its fat-forward sweetness, and its textural yielding to the equation. Cook it to well-done and you have sweet-tart compote sitting on a dry patty, a combination that reads as confused rather than sophisticated. The medium rare center is not optional — it is the substance that makes these flavors mean something.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
225g (1½ cups) pitted prunes (dried plums), roughly chopped
4 slices aged Gruyère or Comté cheese
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BUNS — Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer bowl.
2. Add warm milk, warm water, egg, and butter. Mix with dough hook on low until combined, then medium speed for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
3. Cover and let rise until doubled, about 1 hour.
4. Divide into 4 portions, shape into balls, place on a parchment-lined sheet pan, flatten. Cover and proof 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash. Bake 16–18 minutes until golden. Cool completely on a wire rack.
6. MAKE THE PRUNE-PORT WINE COMPOTE — Combine prunes, port, water, brown sugar, cinnamon stick, cloves, and orange zest in a small saucepan over medium heat.
7. Bring to a simmer and cook, stirring occasionally, for 20–25 minutes until the prunes are very soft and the liquid has reduced to a thick, syrupy glaze.

8. Remove cinnamon stick, cloves, and orange zest. Stir in orange juice and balsamic vinegar. Season with salt. The compote should be thick and spreadable. Let cool. (It thickens further as it cools.)
9. MAKE THE PRUNE MOSTARDA — Combine chopped prunes, white wine, white wine vinegar, and sugar in a small saucepan over medium-low heat.
10. Cook, stirring frequently, until the liquid is absorbed and the mixture is thick and jammy, about 10 minutes.
11. Stir in dry mustard, yellow mustard seeds, and brown mustard seeds. Cook 2 more minutes. Season with salt. Let cool. The mostarda should be chunky, slightly sticky, and sharply flavored.
12. MAKE THE MUSTARD MAYO — Stir together mayonnaise and whole grain mustard. Set aside.

13. FORM THE PATTIES — Divide beef into 4 equal portions (about 170g each). Form into patties ¾-inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.
14. COOK THE PATTIES — Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat with a thin film of neutral oil until smoking.
15. Cook patties undisturbed for 3 minutes until a deep brown crust forms. Flip once.
16. Lay a slice of Gruyère or Comté on each patty. Cook 2–2½ more minutes.
17. Check internal temperature — target 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare.
18. Remove and tent with foil. Rest 3 minutes.
19. TOAST THE BUNS — Split buns and toast cut-side down in the pan over medium heat, 60–90 seconds.
20. ASSEMBLE — Spread mustard mayo on both cut sides of the bun.
21. Place frisée or watercress on the bottom bun.
22. Add shallot slices.
23. Set the cheese-topped patty on the shallots.
24. Spoon a generous tablespoon of prune-port compote over the cheese.
25. Add a smaller spoonful of prune mostarda on top of the compote — it is intensely flavored, so a little goes a long way.
26. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
